# In Praise of Desire Paths

Somewhere near you there is almost certainly a strip of dirt cutting diagonally across a patch of grass. It probably starts at the corner of a sidewalk and ends at a bus stop, a parking lot, or a gap in a hedge. Nobody designed it. No committee approved it. It exists because hundreds or thousands of people, independently and without consulting each other, decided that the official route was a little too long, and that the grass could take it.

Planners call these "desire paths" or "desire lines," and I find them among the most quietly eloquent things in the built world. They are a kind of vote, cast with feet, tallied in bare earth. They record something a survey could never capture: not what people say they want, but what they actually do when they think no one is watching.

Walk across a university campus and you will see the argument playing out in real time. Architects love right angles. They love symmetry, sightlines, the satisfying geometry of a quad bisected by crisp perpendicular walkways. Students, meanwhile, love getting to class. When the two preferences collide, the students win, slowly, one footstep at a time. The grass thins, then yellows, then disappears. Eventually someone puts up a little sign asking people to please stay on the path, and the sign is ignored with the serene indifference that only a large crowd can manage.

Some institutions have learned to stop fighting. There are stories, possibly embellished in the retelling as these stories tend to be, of campuses that deliberately laid down grass and waited a year before paving anything, letting the students show them where the walkways should go. Whether or not every version of that story is true, the idea behind it is sound and a little humbling. It says: we do not fully know how people will use this space, so let us watch before we decide. It treats design as a conversation rather than a decree.

There's a particular kind of intelligence in a desire path that I think is worth dwelling on. No single person creates one. The first walker who cuts across the lawn leaves almost no trace; the grass springs back. The tenth leaves a faint impression. By the hundredth, there is a visible line, and now something interesting happens: the path begins to recruit. People who might have stayed on the sidewalk see the trail and think, *oh, others go that way*, and follow it. The path deepens because it exists, and exists because it deepens. It is a feedback loop, the same basic mechanism by which ants find the shortest route to food, or rivers carve their beds, or a phrase becomes a cliché.

This means desire paths aren't perfectly rational. They reflect not only efficiency but also imitation, habit, and a bit of historical accident. Sometimes a path bends around an obstacle that was removed years ago, the curve preserved like a fossil of a tree that no longer stands. Sometimes two paths braid together, then split, then rejoin, recording some ancient disagreement about the best way to reach the library. Read closely, they are a history of small decisions, layered over time.

I think part of what draws me to them is that they sit right at the boundary between order and freedom, which is where most of the interesting things in life seem to happen. A world with no designed paths at all would be exhausting; you'd have to figure out your route every time, bushwhacking through the undergrowth of every decision. But a world where the designed paths were perfectly enforced would be a kind of prison, however pleasant the landscaping. Desire paths are what happens when structure is strong enough to be useful but loose enough to be revised. They're the margin notes people write in the book of the city.

The metaphor extends easily, maybe too easily, but I'll indulge it anyway. Language has desire paths. The rules of grammar lay down the official walkways, and speakers, over generations, wear shortcuts across them. "Going to" becomes "gonna." "Do not" becomes "don't." Grammarians put up the little signs, and the signs are ignored, and eventually the shortcuts get paved into the dictionary. What was once a sloppy deviation becomes the standard route, and the next generation cuts new corners of its own.

Software has them too. Engineers build a feature intending it to be used one way, and users immediately find some other way, sometimes an ingenious hack the designers never imagined. The smart companies watch for this. The hashtag, famously, started as a convention invented by users, which the platform later adopted and built into the product. That's a desire path getting paved.

Even personal lives have them. We are handed certain routes: go to school, pick a career, follow the sequence. And many people walk those routes contentedly, which is fine; sidewalks exist for good reasons. But most lives, looked at closely, contain at least a few diagonal cuts across the lawn, places where someone looked at the prescribed path and thought, *that's the long way around for me*, and stepped onto the grass.

What I appreciate most, though, is the humility that desire paths demand of anyone who designs things. They are a standing reminder that the people who use a system know things the people who build it don't. The planner in the office sees a clean diagram; the person running late for the bus sees forty unnecessary meters of concrete. Both perspectives are real, but only one of them is getting rained on at 7:45 in the morning.

There is a line of thinking, reportedly practiced in parts of Finland, of photographing footprints in fresh snow to see where people naturally want to walk before deciding where to build paths. I love this image: a city waiting for winter so it can read the footprints and learn what its citizens were trying to tell it all along. Snow as a blank page. Walkers as authors. The planner as, finally, a reader.

The grass will always lose, eventually. That's fine. It was never really about the grass.
